overview: This file combines a substantive 1931 diplomatic despatch and translated Japanese immigration ordinances with several later cross-reference sheets concerning related records. Ambassador William Cameron Forbes forwarded regulations governing the entry of aliens into Japan and the Japanese South Seas Mandate, covering passports, visas, exclusion, deportation, public health, public order, and exemptions for diplomats, officials, and ships’ crews; he also noted that regulations for the Kwantung Leased Territory and South Manchuria Railway Zone had been sent from Dairen in 1918. The remaining sheets point to records on Kwantung residence, trade, travel, and temporary employment, as well as 1934–1935 State Department instructions seeking permission to publish related correspondence in Foreign Relations of the United States.
keywords: Foreign Relations of the United States

subfiles.from: William Cameron Forbes, U.S. Embassy in Japan
subfiles.about: The sheet directs researchers to Despatch No. 179 concerning laws governing alien entry into Japan and the South Sea Islands of Japan.
subfiles.summary: This filing note cross-references Despatch No. 179 under another decimal-file location. It identifies Forbes as the reporting officer and states that the despatch enclosed translated copies of the applicable alien-entry laws.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 179 transmitting Japanese alien-entry laws
subfiles.from: William Cameron Forbes, U.S. Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.about: Forbes transmits translations of the laws regulating alien entry into Japan and the South Sea Islands.
subfiles.summary: Responding to the Department’s circular instruction of January 3, 1931, Forbes forwards two translated sets of alien-entry regulations. He explains that a translation of the corresponding law for the Kwantung Leased Territory and Railway Zone had already been transmitted by the American consul at Dairen in a despatch dated March 28, 1918.

subfiles.title: Regulations governing the entry of aliens into Japan
subfiles.about: The translated ordinance establishes documentary requirements, grounds for exclusion, enforcement powers, and exemptions governing aliens entering Japan.
subfiles.summary: The regulation permits prefectural governors to exclude foreigners lacking valid documents or considered threats to security, public order, morality, public health, or public finances. Passports or nationality certificates generally require photographs and Japanese consular visas, subject to reciprocal exemptions. Aliens must show documents and answer police inquiries truthfully, while fraud or noncompliance can lead to exclusion or deportation. Diplomats, foreign officials, their families, and crews of foreign ships are exempted.

subfiles.title: Regulations concerning alien entry into the South Sea Islands
subfiles.about: The translated ordinance applies Japanese alien-entry controls to the South Sea Islands administered by Japan.
subfiles.summary: The ordinance authorizes branch-office chiefs to bar aliens lacking proper documents or deemed dangerous to imperial welfare, public peace, morals, health, or public finances. It specifies photographic passports or nationality certificates and Japanese consular visas, while allowing reciprocal exemptions and an exception for arrivals from elsewhere in the Empire. False statements, document misuse, or fraudulent visas can result in exclusion or deportation. Diplomats, official travelers, their families, and foreign ships’ crews are exempt; the ordinance was gazetted on May 13, 1925.

interest: The file is useful for tracing how metropolitan Japanese immigration controls were adapted to colonial and leased territories, particularly the South Seas Mandate and Kwantung. Its translated ordinances reveal the broad administrative discretion exercised through security, morality, health, poverty, and documentary criteria, while their reciprocity clauses and diplomatic and maritime exemptions illuminate the international dimensions of border control. The cross-reference sheets are also valuable evidence of State Department filing practices and of the diplomatic clearance process used in the 1930s when preparing earlier correspondence for publication in Foreign Relations of the United States.
